headings.title: Defining Drug Compliance and Adherence
headings.content: Drug compliance refers to how closely a patient follows the prescribed routine of taking medication, including the right dose, timing, and frequency. Adherence implies a more collaborative relationship where the patient actively participates in their treatment plan rather than passively obeying instructions. When patients stop taking drugs prematurely or skip doses, therapeutic goals fail and conditions worsen. Nurses must understand these terms to properly evaluate how well a patient manages their therapy at home.

headings.title: Clinical Importance of Medication Adherence
headings.content: Consistent medication intake maintains steady drug plasma levels required for clinical efficacy. Poor adherence leads to treatment failure, disease progression, antimicrobial resistance, and avoidable hospital admissions. Chronic conditions like hypertension and diabetes demand lifelong daily regimens where missing doses triggers severe complications such as stroke or kidney failure. Monitoring adherence safeguards the health investments made by both the patient and the healthcare system.

headings.title: Local Factors Influencing Non-Compliance in Nigeria
headings.content:
- **Financial constraints**: Out-of-pocket spending for drugs forces many patients to miss doses or buy incomplete doses.
- **Traditional and religious beliefs**: Reliance on herbal preparations and spiritual healing houses often delays or replaces orthodox treatment.
- **Transportation costs**: Long distances to healthcare facilities make clinic visits and drug refilling difficult.
- **Drug availability**: Frequent stockouts in public health facilities force patients to source medications from unregulated open drug markets.

headings.title: Barriers to Medication Adherence
headings.content: Complex drug regimens involving multiple daily pills confuse patients and increase omission rates. Adverse drug reactions discourage continuation, especially when patients are not forewarned about minor side effects. Cognitive impairment, forgetfulness, and poor health literacy further compound the problem. When patients do not understand how a drug works, they see little value in tolerating its side effects or spending money on it.

headings.title: Assessment Methods for Compliance
headings.content:
Evaluating adherence requires a combination of subjective and objective approaches since patients often overstate how well they take their drugs. 

| Method | Description | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **Self-report** | Asking the patient directly about their pill-taking habits | Subject to recall bias and social desirability | 
| **Pill count** | Counting remaining tablets returned in the container | Patients can manipulate counts before visits |
| **Biological assay** | Measuring drug levels in blood or urine | Costly and reflects only recent intake |

headings.title: Patient Education and Counselling Strategies
headings.content: Effective education bridges the gap between prescription and practice. Nurses must use simple, non-medical language, avoiding clinical jargon. Tailoring instructions to fit the patient's daily routine, such as linking pill-taking to breakfast or bedtime, improves consistency. Encouraging the teach-back method ensures the patient truly understands the dosage schedule before leaving the clinic.

headings.title: Interventions to Improve Drug Adherence
headings.content: Practical tools and systematic support structures help sustain long-term compliance. Pill organizers, alarm reminders on mobile phones, and calendar charts assist patients with complex schedules. Simplifying regimens through once-daily combination pills reduces the pill burden. Involving family members or caregivers also provides a support system that encourages the patient to stay on track.

headings.title: The Role of the Nurse in Managing Non-Compliance
headings.content: Nurses act as advocates, educators, and monitors in managing medication adherence. Building a trusting, non-judgmental relationship encourages patients to confess when they miss doses without fear of reprimand. Nurses coordinate care with pharmacists and physicians to adjust regimens that clash with a patient's lifestyle or financial status. Continuous assessment and empathetic support remain the core tools for long-term success.
